title: Diagnose connections
intro: Use Diagnose when a saved host connector cannot connect. It checks the settings, server name, port, login and server version in order.
You need Manage connectors. Diagnosis runs from the OpenLDR server using stored credentials. It opens a test connection but does not import data.
Use your own saved connection. The pictures show a real isolated Postgres connection and a deliberately absent SQL Server instance. A failed example does not prove a SQL Server login works.

tasks.title: Diagnose a saved connection
intro: Begin with a connection you already use, or the warehouse connector on a new installation.
steps: Open the host connector row dots and select Diagnose. Checks start as the sheet opens.
Read the status and message for each step. A warning gives advice without stopping the later checks.
Check Port, Login and Server version. The local Postgres example passes all checks.
Open the diagnosis sheet dots and select Run again. This uses the currently saved settings.
tasks.result: A successful run ends with All checks passed. It proves the tested connection. It does not prove a particular report query, source schema or account permission.

tasks.title: Enter SQL Server settings
intro: Ask the database operator whether you have a named instance, a fixed TCP port, a SQL login or a Windows domain account. Do not create the fictional connection unless you want an isolated failure example.
steps: Close the diagnosis sheet. Open the Connectors page dots and choose Add connector. Enter a useful name and set Category to Host.
Enter Host. A pasted SERVER\INSTANCE splits into Host and Instance name when you leave the field. Use a fixed Port only when Instance name is empty.
Fill Database, User and Password. For a Windows account, fill Windows domain and use the username without the domain. Leave the domain blank for a SQL login.
Encrypt starts on. Use the server operator's encryption and certificate requirements. Trust server certificate accepts a server certificate without normal certificate validation.
Open the sheet dots and choose Save.
tasks.result: The saved connector can now be diagnosed. The screenshot example intentionally names an instance that does not exist.

tasks.title: Read and correct a failed diagnosis
intro: Diagnosis stops at the first failed check. Later steps show as skipped, so they have no result yet.
steps: Open its row dots and choose Diagnose.
Read the failed step and correction message. This example gets no SQL Server Browser reply for its absent named instance.
Here Port, Login and Server version were not attempted. Do not treat a skipped login as an accepted password.

Close diagnosis, open row dots and choose Edit. Check Host and Instance name. If your operator supplies a fixed TCP port, clear Instance name and enter that port. Save any change, then diagnose again.
tasks.result: Follow the actual failed step. The correction can require a database service, firewall or name-resolution change outside OpenLDR. This preview does not claim the absent instance was repaired.

tasks.title: Read diagnosis on a phone
intro: The same row menu opens diagnosis at phone width.
steps: Open Diagnose, then scroll inside the sheet to read each result. Messages wrap beneath the step name.

end.title: What the checks mean
paragraphs: Settings. A host is present and the port is valid. A localhost warning reminds you that Docker containers have their own loopback address.
Server name. The OpenLDR server resolves the name to an address. A successful lookup does not prove the database port answers.
SQL Server Browser. For a named SQL Server instance, UDP 1434 reports its TCP port. Ask the operator to start Browser and allow UDP, or use the actual fixed TCP port with no instance name.
Port. A TCP connection opens. A wrong service can still answer the port.
Login. The saved account opens the database. Check username, password, domain and database access when this fails.
Server version. The server answers a small query. This still does not prove the tables or columns required by an importer exist.

end.title: Run the same check from the CLI
paragraphs: Follow Start here for CLI setup. From openldr_ce, list connectors to get the id. Diagnose exits 1 when a step fails. Add --json for structured results.
html:
pnpm openldr connectors list
pnpm openldr connectors diagnose <id>
pnpm openldr connectors diagnose <id> --json

end.title: Optional practice and limits
paragraphs: No sample data is needed. Test your existing warehouse connector first. A disposable Microsoft SQL connector with a nonexistent instance can demonstrate the Browser failure. Remove that example afterward through its row dots and confirmation.

This preview exercised actual Postgres success and a real UDP timeout for an absent named instance. It did not exercise Windows authentication, a working named SQL Server instance, certificate replacement or an old TLS server.

end.title: Troubleshooting
paragraphs: The first check fails. Read that check before the skipped results. Correct the saved settings in Edit and run Diagnose again.
Browser times out for a named SQL Server instance. Check the server and instance names and whether SQL Server Browser is reachable. Later checks are skipped until discovery succeeds.
All checks pass but the importer fails. Diagnosis verifies the connection and server response. It does not prove that the account can read each required source table.

end.title: Related guides
paragraphs: Connectors covers creation, testing and secret changes. Import from OpenLDR v1 uses a database connector.
